newsitem.title: USA: U.S. hopeful N. Korea will join peace talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. hopeful N. Korea will join peace talks.

text.p: The United States said after day-long talks on Wednesday that it was hopeful North Korea would agree to join formal negotiations on a permanent peace treaty with South Korea.

"There were no breakthroughs but the United States is hopeful that today's talks will lead to North Koera joining the formal four-party talks that were proposed by President Bill Clinton and (South Korean) President Kim (Young-sam) last April," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.

He spoke at the conclusion of preliminary talks in New York involving the United States, South Korea and North Korea that marked the first time the bitter Korean rivals had sat down together to discuss ending their peninsula's technical state of war.

North Korea asked for the New York meeting -- called a "joint briefing" by Washington -- to learn more about the U.S.-South Korean proposal. Should formal peace talks get underway, China would also be included.

Burns, briefing reporters at the State Department, called the New York talks "serious and sincere, very businesslike." He said "throughout the day, our delegation felt that both South and North Korean delegates acquitted themselves in a very responsible, businesslike serious way."

The three parties covered a broad range of political and economic issues centering on the peace talks proposals. The North Korean delegation, which asked questions about the U.S.-South Korean proposal during the talks, now plans to report to Pyonyang on the discussions, Burns said.
"We believe the United States and South Korea made a sincere and fair proposal and frankly, we don't see any reason why the North Koreans won't respond to it," the spokesman added.

Ahead of the "briefing," a senior U.S. official had said he did not expect an immediate answer from Pyongyang and did not expect formal peace negotiations, in any event, to start until July or thereafter because of events surrounding the third anniversary of North Korean leader Kim Il-sung's death.

On Thursday, the head of the U.S. delegation, deputy assistant secretary of state Charles Kartman, will hold a bilateral meeting with the South Korean team. On Friday, he holds a bilateral meeting with the North Koreans.
Witnesses said Wednesday's meeting began with members of the delegations shaking hands and exchanging small talk, either in Korean or through interpreters.
The three heads of delegation clasped their hands together, one on top of the other, before sitting down at a circular table in a hotel conference room.

It was the first time officials from Pyongyang and Seoul had met to discuss armistice issues although representatives have met on other topics, most notably an international agreement to freeze North Korea's nuclear programme.

The meeting came during a tense period between North and South Korea, including a string of defections from the North and reports of famine and economic collapse in the Stalinist state long allied with China and the former Soviet Union.
The talks stemmed from last April's proposal to North Korea by Clinton and Kim for four-way talks to work out a permanent peace agreement to replace the armistice that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.

North Korea twice delayed taking part in the New York briefing in what was seen as an effort to press Washington to provide more food aid. Pyongyang had demanded that the armistice be scrapped to pave the way for a peace treaty with Washington alone -- a demand that is unacceptable to South Korea and to the United States, which fought at its side during the war, while China supported North Korea.

During a picture-taking session at the start of the briefing, the South Korean delegation head, Deputy Minister for Political Affairs Song Young Shik, told North Korean counterpart Kim Gye Gwan "this is a significant event," to which Kim appeared to indicate concurrence. Kim is vice minister for foreign affairs.
Delegation members, all dressed in dark business suits, were seated at circular tables.
